title_original: How Palestinian Journalists and Photojournalists in Gaza Became the Only Witnesses to Their Own War
excerpt_original: Journalism is Not a Crime is a historic volume honoring the Palestinian journalists who have documented the destruction of Gaza. Spanning from October 7, 2023, through the end of 2025, the book brings together 166 photographs and 70 Instagram posts to create a chronological…

blocks.text: Since the surprise Hamas attack in Israel on October 7, 2023 and the start of the War in Gaza, the territory has faced widespread and systematic destruction . Hospitals have been targeted, cultural heritage sites have been damaged, and whole neighborhoods of civilian housing have been reduced to piles of rubble. The civilian death toll stands at more than 70,000.

With major media outlets banned from Gaza, the work to document and show the world what is going on has fallen almost exclusively on the shoulders of Palestinian journalists and photojournalists. Social media has allowed them to provide an uncensored visual record of the war for anyone to see.

blocks.text: Now, in the new book Journalism is Not a Crime , the journalists working to cover Gaza have a new outlet to show their important work. The work collected spans October 7th, 2023, through the end of 2025, and includes the work of 60 living photojournalists and journalists, while 20 deceased journalists are commemorated through their photographs, final messages, will and private media posts.

“The loss of life by journalists in this war is staggering and needs to be recognized,” FotoEvidence Photo Editor Sarah Lean tells me. “The commitment the Gazan journalists have made to telling this story goes beyond hardship, starvations, loss of friends and family; it extends to their very own lives.”

According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), since the start of the War in Gaza, 191 journalists have been killed by Israel as of September 24, 2026. 2025 marked the highest number of journalists killed since the CPJ began keeping records over 30 years ago. They recorded 129 journalists killed overall, 2/3 of them by Israel , for a total of 86. The second highest year on record was 2024 , when at least 124 journalists were killed, 60% of whom were killed in Israeli attacks.

blocks.text: “We started with no existing archive and no complete list of photographers. Aruallan began identifying Palestinian journalists and photojournalists reporting from Gaza, particularly through Instagram, which became an essential source for our research,” Creative Director Svetlana Bachevanova explains to me. “When a journalist was killed, we went back through their archive, looking not only at their final posts but at their lives, families and work. We wanted to remember them as people, not just as names on a list.”

blocks.text: Aruallan, a photojournalist and researcher, began contacting photographers on their list after the October 10, 2025 ceasefire in Gaza using Instagram, WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram and through mutual contacts. But while contact was a bit easier as communications had stabilized, sometimes finding the original work was a lot more complicated.

For those who had been killed, sometimes it was when their home or workplace had been bombed, meaning that their computers, hard drives, and other archive materials would have been destroyed as well. In other cases, while the families of those who had been killed could be reached, finding their work was not always as simple.

“Even photographers who survived had often been unable to preserve their work properly. Storage was, and remains, expensive, and internet connections were too poor to upload large RAW files to the cloud,” Aruallan tells me. “Some had switched from RAW to JPEG to save space on their memory cards; others had deleted older photographs simply to continue shooting. So reaching the photographer, or their family, did not necessarily mean that the original file still existed or could be transferred.”

This is why some of the photographs in the book are screenshots instead of original high-resolution works: they are not just lower quality substitutes; they are the only version of the work that still exists. These images are also the evidence of the conditions under which the reporters work, and of how they must save their work and transmit it out of Gaza.

blocks.text: Throughout the War, the duty of the journalists did not waver. They lost homes, relatives, and colleagues. They were displaced over and over again as the lines of battle shifted. They worried about their families, and themselves. Food became scarce, and starvation was a real fear. But they all continued working, knowing they could be killed at any time, while sharing the truth of what was going on through their reporting.

“Journalists should not be killed for doing their job. If we fail to stand up when journalists are killed for reporting, we risk allowing this to become a new normal, not only in Gaza, but in conflicts everywhere,” Bachevanova explains. “That should concern all of us, because when journalists can no longer bear witness safely, we all lose access to the truth.”

blocks.text: Journalism is Not a Crime is published as part of the 2026 FotoEvidence Book Award. It can be purchased through their website .
